newsitem.title: USA: U.S. food aid for N. Korea expected Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: U.S. food aid for N. Korea expected Tuesday.

text.p: The United States on Monday set a date for talks with North Korea on missile sales and promised an announcement on new food aid for Pyongyang before Wednesday's critical meeting on proposed peace talks.
The last U.S. food donation was $10 million made public in February. A senior official said the new donation would be "significant" but he declined to disclose the exact amount.

Private aid groups said if Washington only gave another $10 million in response to a United Nations appeal for $95.5 million, it would be a pittance compared to what is needed to stave off the famine threatening North Koera.

"The United States is now finishing its internal deliberations on the issue of whether or not to respond to the augmented appeal of the World Food Programme for a greater level of food assistance to North Korea, and I would expect within the next 24 hours that I will have an announcement to make on that issue," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
The World Food Programme has called for $95.5 million for 200,000 tons of food. Washington has provided $18.4 million since late 1995, including a $10 million donation now being shipped to Pyongyang.
Burns said the United States and North Korea had also agreed to hold talks in New York on May 12-13 to discuss U.S. concerns over North Korea's reported exports of missiles.
He told a news briefing a U.S. team led by Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Robert Einhorn wanted to discuss reports of "various allegations of sales and transfers."

Japan's foreign minister highlighted North Korea's potential threat to Asia on Monday by citing unconfirmed reports that Pyongyang may have deployed some of its Rodong-I ballistic missiles capable of hitting most of Japan.
Burns said he was unable to confirm whether or not that missile has been deployed.

But he said: "We have concerns, not only about that missile but about various missile related activity of the North Koreans. And that is why we have sought and have now achieved a scheduling of a meeting with the North Koreans ... to discuss a variety of these concerns."

Experts say Pyongyang has already provided short-range Scud missiles to Iran and Syria, ballistic missile technology to Iran, Syria and Egypt and discussed the sale of intermediate range missiles, including the Rodong-I, with Iran, Syria and Libya.

On Wednesday, the United States hopes to receive at a meeting in New York with North and South Korean officals a response from Pyongyang to a U.S.-South Korean proposal for four-way peace talks on the future of Korea.
The aim is to conclude a peace treaty that would finally close the books on the 1950-53 Korean War.

There might not be a clear-cut answer from the North Koreans on Wednesday and the talks may spill over into Friday, Burns said. The chief U.S. negotiator, Charles Kartman, has to be in Washington to testify before Congress on Thursday.

Burns denied food aid was being used to elicit a positive response from North Korea. But U.S. officials have acknowledged food shortages have become such a problem that North Korean officials refused to consider the peace talk proposal without assurances at least some emergency food was forthcoming.
The spokesman refused to say if the United States might be prepared to ease trade sanctions on North Korea if Pyongyang agrees this week to join the four-party peace talks.

"Let's just take it one step at a time. If we get a positive answer, we'll obviously try to begin those talks with the Chinese government and the others, and see how relations develop from there. But I don't want to predict what steps we would take," he said.

After some scepticism about the problem, the Clinton administration and members of Congress have increasingly expressed public concerns about a severe food shortage in North Korea, caused in large part by two years of floods.

Burns, asked about the trend, said "by all accounts, the situation is worsening. It is dramatically worse than it was several months ago or even four or five weeks ago. At least our assessment of it is dramatically worse."
